chapters.title: Soul and Body, Wished Together
chapters.teaser: John's famous greeting to Gaius ties physical health to a soul that's already thriving.
body: "I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (v.2) is a warm, ordinary ancient greeting, lifted by its second half. The comparison only works because something is already established: Gaius's soul genuinely is prospering, shown by the report that follows of his faithful life and generous hospitality (v.3-6).

This single verse has sometimes been stretched into a blanket promise of material wealth for the faithful, pulled loose from its context. Read plainly, it's just a personal letter's opening kindness — one that still assumes spiritual health, love of truth, and a well-lived life are the deeper, prior reality any wish for outward wellbeing rests on.

chapters.title: Hospitality as Gospel Partnership
chapters.teaser: Gaius is praised for supporting traveling missionaries who took nothing from outsiders.
body: "Thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers" (v.5) praises Gaius for taking in itinerant workers he'd likely never met — a genuine risk and cost in the ancient world, where travel meant depending entirely on local believers for food, shelter, and safe passage.

Verse 7 explains why that support mattered so much: these workers went out for Christ's name, refusing to take anything from pagan patrons who might have compromised or obligated them. That left Christian hospitality as their only real lifeline. Receiving them, John concludes, made the host an active partner in the mission itself (v.8), not just someone offering well-wishes from the sidelines.

chapters.title: Diotrephes and Local Church Politics
chapters.teaser: A named troublemaker gives a rare, candid glimpse into conflict inside an early congregation.
body: A real name and a real grievance show up in such a short letter: Diotrephes, who "loveth to have the preeminence" among the believers, won't even receive John himself (v.9). This isn't abstract false teaching like the antichrists of 1 and 2 John — it's a straightforward power struggle over leadership.

The charges are specific: Diotrephes spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome traveling believers, and even throws people out of the church for trying to host them anyway (v.10). It's a sobering reminder that the early church's dangers weren't only doctrinal error from outsiders — plain ambition and control inside a congregation could choke out hospitality and truth just as easily.

chapters.title: Follow What Is Good
chapters.teaser: John reduces the letter's tension to a simple moral principle: imitate good, not evil.
body: Right after the account of Diotrephes, John sets down the letter's ethical center of gravity: imitate good, not evil, because doing good marks someone as being of God, and doing evil means never having truly seen him (v.11). Addressed to Gaius, it clearly functions as a broader test too — a way of telling real spiritual sight from its absence.

The principle is almost understated, and that's exactly the point. After cataloguing hospitality, mission support, and one leader's petty tyranny, John doesn't reach for a complicated theological resolution — he hands readers a rule anyone can apply immediately: watch what a person actually does.

chapters.title: Demetrius, the Counter-Example
chapters.teaser: A second named figure closes the letter as the positive mirror image of Diotrephes.
body: Demetrius gets the opposite treatment from Diotrephes: a good report from everyone, and from the truth itself, with John adding his own testimony on top (v.12). The placement is deliberate — one man grasping for preeminence and shutting others out, the other apparently commended on every side.

The letter closes almost exactly like 2 John, preferring presence over paper: John has much more to say, but would rather say it face to face than fill more pages with ink (v.13-14). Even in a letter partly about conflict and correction, the last word is peace and the hope of a real reunion — a fittingly personal close to the most personal letter in the New Testament.
